chapter_theme: The Chera king vows to bring a stone for a god from the Himalaya on the heads of the northern kings who scorned Tamil strength, marches north with Siva's feet on his crown, is charged by sky-faring sages to protect the northern Brahmins, refuses his allies' offer of a stone, crosses the Ganga, defeats the Aryan kings and captures Kanakan and Vijayan, while the demons hail his battlefield as a field of dharma; he then takes the stone for the pathini.

cast.role: the Chera king of Vanji who leads the northern expedition for the pathini's stone (also குட்டுவன், வானவன், காவலன் here)
the king's preceptor, who counsels him to calm his anger
the royal astrologer, master of the five branches of reckoning, who fixes the hour of departure
the assembled warriors and chiefs whom the king addresses
the king's councils and officers, who take the sword and umbrella to the outer shrine
those who bring the prasada of the god reclining on the serpent
the dancing women of Vanji, who bless the departing king
the court praisers who hail the king as he sets out
sages who travel through the sky and stop at the camp on their way to Malaya
performers from Konkan and Karnataka who sing at the camp
performers of the western hills (Kudagu) who sing the rainy-season kuravai
praise-singers who hail the king
the gatekeepers who announce the envoys
chief of the envoys sent by the Nootruvar Kannar
northern rulers allied with the Chera, who supply the boats to cross the Ganga
the thousand robed officers who bring gifts and tribute
the scribes who hand sealed letters to the kings
son of Balakumaran, a northern king who scorned Tamil strength
son of Balakumaran, Kanakan's brother and ally
the northern (Aryan) kings Uttaran, Vichitran, Rudran, Bhairavan, Chitran, Singan, Dhanuttaran, Svetan and others who fight the Chera
the demon women of the battlefield, who dance, sing and cook the battle feast
the Chera's commander, with whom he completes the campaign

silappathikaram:26:1-18.reading: After the drum proclaims the campaign, the king takes the lion throne before his preceptor, astrologer, ministers and generals and vows that, since the boast of the northern kings reported to him by the Himalayan ascetics would shame kings like him if it went unanswered, his sword will not come back empty without a stone, laid on the crowned heads of the northern kings, from which to carve a god, or else let him be a king whose sceptre makes his own people tremble instead of his foes.
silappathikaram:26:1-18.nuance: The vow is in the old conditional form: the penalty he accepts is not death or loss in battle but becoming a cruel king to his own subjects, so the fear his sceptre must cause is either the enemy's or his people's. The insult is only reported, carried by ascetics from the Himalaya (இமையத் தாபதர்), and அமையா வாழ்க்கை அரைசர் may mean kings of restless or unworthy life; the words of the boast are not given here. The god to be carved is not yet named as Kannaki in these lines.
silappathikaram:26:1-18.unit_note: End moved from line 22 to line 18: the king's vow closes with ஆகென on line 18, and lines 19-24 are the preceptor's reply, which ends with ஆசான் கூற on line 24.
silappathikaram:26:1-18.event: The Chera king, enthroned before his council, vows to bring back a stone for a god on the heads of the northern kings or be a tyrant to his own people.

claims.claim: an insult to kings left unanswered brings disgrace on every king like the one insulted
a king who fails his war vow deserves to become a king whose sceptre terrifies his own subjects

silappathikaram:26:19-31.reading: The preceptor asks whether any king, besides the Chola and Pandya who wear the aar and the neem, would stand against his vow, tells him that those two have not scorned him and bids his anger settle; then the astrologer, master of the five branches of reckoning, rises to hail his victory and declares that this very moment is the auspicious hour for marching in the chosen direction.
silappathikaram:26:19-31.nuance: The preceptor's counsel is double: it flatters (no northern king can face you) and restrains (the only equals, the other two Tamil crowns, are not the offenders), so the anger is turned wholly north. The astrologer's முழுத்தம் makes the departure an act of timing as much as of will.
silappathikaram:26:19-31.unit_note: Start moved from line 23 to line 19 (see the previous unit) and end from line 38 to line 31: the astrologer's speech closes with என்று ஏத்த on line 31, and line 32 begins the king's response.
silappathikaram:26:19-31.event: The preceptor calms the king's anger and the astrologer declares the hour for setting out north.

silappathikaram:26:32-53.reading: Hearing the astrologer, the king orders his sword and umbrella moved northward; with drums roaring, the councils and officers hail him, carry the sword and white umbrella on an elephant's neck into the outer shrine, the king who strings the vanji with the palmyra feasts his eager generals with the great rice, wears on his crown the vanji that blossoms in flowerless Vanji, and the morning drum sounds at the gate.
silappathikaram:26:32-53.nuance: பூவா வஞ்சியிற் பூத்த வஞ்சி plays on the city's name and the vanji flower worn for an invading march: the garland of conquest is said to bloom in a city that bears the flower's name but not the flower. The great rice (பெருஞ்சோறு) shared with the generals binds them to the campaign before it starts.
silappathikaram:26:32-53.unit_note: Start moved from line 39 to line 32 (see the previous unit): the king hears and gives the order at lines 32-33, and the long sentence of preparations closes with எழுதலும் on line 53.
silappathikaram:26:32-53.event: The sword and umbrella are moved north to the outer shrine, the generals are feasted with the great rice, and the king puts on the vanji garland.

silappathikaram:26:54-73.reading: The king sets the feet of the moon-crowned god who fills the world upon his head with the vanji garland, bows the head that bows to no one, circles the shrine and mounts his war elephant amid the Brahmins' oblation smoke; when some bring the prasada of the god who sleeps on the serpent in the golden hall, he takes it on his shoulder, since Siva's feet are on his crown, and the dancing women everywhere bless him to go with the victor's flowers on his elephant's brow.
silappathikaram:26:54-73.nuance: The king worships both gods but ranks them on his body: the matted god's feet on the crown, Vishnu's prasada on the shoulder, and the narrator gives the reason (வைத்தலின்) without comment. இறைஞ்சாச் சென்னி இறைஞ்சி: the head that bows to no king bows to the god. ஆடக மாடம் may name a particular Vishnu shrine; the lines do not say which.
silappathikaram:26:54-73.unit_note: Start unchanged at line 54; end moved from line 69 to line 73: the dancing women's blessing, begun at line 68, closes with ஆகென on line 73.
silappathikaram:26:54-73.event: The king worships Siva before setting out, takes Vishnu's prasada on his shoulder, and is blessed by the dancing women.

silappathikaram:26:74-92.reading: Bards, panegyrists and heralds, elephant riders, horse captains and sword warriors hail him; like Indra leaving his city against the asuras he leaves Vanji, his army spreading like a white-crested sea, bending mountain backs and cutting paths through the land, camps on the slopes of the Nilagiri, and, praised by his men, lies down on the great couch amid the din of the moving army.
silappathikaram:26:74-92.nuance: The comparison with Indra marching on the asuras makes the northern kings the demons of the simile before any battle is fought.
silappathikaram:26:74-92.unit_note: Start moved from line 70 to line 74 (see the previous unit) and end from line 94 to line 92: the march and the camp close at line 92, and the sky-faring sages' descent, begun at line 93, runs to line 97.
silappathikaram:26:74-92.event: Praised by bards and soldiers, the king marches out of Vanji and camps at the Nilagiri.

silappathikaram:26:93-104.reading: Sages who travel the sky, wishing to see the Indra-like ruler, descend into the hall where the king rises and bows to them, and tell the Vanavan born in Vanji by the grace of the red-haired god that they are going to Malaya, and since his purpose is the great Himalaya, where Brahmins of the hard Vedas live, guarding them is his duty; they bless him and leave.
silappathikaram:26:93-104.nuance: The sages turn the campaign's road into a duty: on the way to punish northern kings, the Chera is charged to protect the northern Brahmins. He keeps the charge at the close of the kaathai (lines 248-250), when he orders the Veda-keepers of the north guarded before he takes the stone.
silappathikaram:26:93-104.unit_note: Start moved from line 95 to line 93 and end from line 106 to line 104: the sages' descent begins with விசும்பியங்கு முனிவர் on line 93, and their speech and departure close with போந்ததற் பின்னர் on line 104.
silappathikaram:26:93-104.event: Sky-faring sages visit the camp and charge the king to protect the Brahmins of the Himalaya.

claims.claim: protecting the Brahmins who keep the Vedas is a king's duty

silappathikaram:26:105-127.reading: Performers from Konkan and Karnataka in the dress of their peoples come with dark-eyed women singing that spring has come and the lover has not, the Kudagar come singing the rainy-season kuravai, asking a bangled girl whether it is the rain cloud that has come or her lover's chariot with his work done, and the Ovar hail the king who will finish his sword-work to live an aeon; he rewards them all with jewels beyond their hopes.
silappathikaram:26:105-127.nuance: The camp's songs are songs of separation sung to a man setting out: the spring song says the lover has not come, the rain song imagines his chariot returning with his work done (செய்வினை முடித்து), so the performers set the king's campaign in the frame of a woman waiting for the return. கூத்துள் படுவோன் காட்டிய முறைமையின் may mean the rewards followed the rule the dance-master showed; the phrase is not clear.
silappathikaram:26:105-127.unit_note: Start moved from line 107 to line 105 and end from line 128 to line 127: the new scene begins after போந்ததற் பின்னர் on line 104, and the king's gifts close the scene at line 127; line 128 begins the gatekeepers' list.
silappathikaram:26:105-127.event: Performers from Konkan, Karnataka and Kudagu sing at the camp and the king rewards them.

silappathikaram:26:128-140.reading: The gatekeepers announce to the king of the bow banner that there have arrived one hundred and two dancing women, two hundred and eight musicians, a hundred jesters versed in the ninety-six kinds of sect, a hundred chariots, five hundred elephants, ten thousand horses, twenty thousand carts of northern goods marked in writing, and a thousand robed officers led by Sanjayan.
silappathikaram:26:128-140.nuance: தொண்ணூற் றறுவகைப் பாசண்டத் துறை நண்ணிய நூற்றுவர் நகைவேழம்பர்: the jesters are said to know the ninety-six sects, perhaps because their comedy imitates the sects' teachers; the number ninety-six is the conventional count of the heterodox schools, but the line does not say how the jesters use it.
silappathikaram:26:128-140.unit_note: Start moved from line 129 to line 128 (see the previous unit) and end from line 139 to line 140: the gatekeepers' announcement closes with வாயிலோர் என on line 140.
silappathikaram:26:128-140.event: The gatekeepers announce the arrival of the allied envoys and their gifts.

silappathikaram:26:141-155.reading: The king bids the dancers, performers and musicians come in with Sanjayan; Sanjayan enters, bows, presents the hundred and two and the craftsmen, and reports the Nootruvar Kannar's message that if the Chera's march north is only for a stone to carve a god, they themselves will take one from the Himalaya, bathe it in the Ganga and bring it to him.
silappathikaram:26:141-155.nuance: The allies' offer would give the king his stone without a war; the next unit declines it, so the stone must be taken by battle for the vow to be kept, not merely obtained.
silappathikaram:26:141-155.unit_note: Start moved from line 140 to line 141 (see the previous unit) and end from line 149 to line 155: Sanjayan's report of the Kannar's offer closes with என்றனர் என்று ... வாழ்கென on lines 154-155.
silappathikaram:26:141-155.event: Sanjayan presents the gifts and reports the Nootruvar Kannar's offer to fetch and bathe the stone for the king.

silappathikaram:26:156-171.reading: The king answers that Kanakan and Vijayan, the sons of Balakumaran, of unguarded tongue, joined with visiting kings, have not known the strength of Tamil; let Sanjayan tell the Kannar that an army like Death is coming and have them build rows of boats to cross the Ganga; Sanjayan leaves, and the thousand robed officers bring sandal, pearls and the Pandya's tribute, while the scribes hand the kings sealed letters.
silappathikaram:26:156-171.nuance: The insult is now named: two kings, Kanakan and Vijayan, whose fault is a careless tongue (காவா நாவின்) and ignorance of அருந்தமிழ் ஆற்றல். The quarrel is cast as the honour of Tamil, not of the Chera alone, which is why the Pandya's tribute arrives in the same breath.
silappathikaram:26:156-171.unit_note: Start moved from line 150 to line 156 (see the previous unit) and end from line 168 to line 171: the delivery of gifts and letters closes with அளித்தாங்கு on line 171.
silappathikaram:26:156-171.event: The king refuses the allies' stone, names Kanakan and Vijayan as the offenders, and asks the Kannar for boats to cross the Ganga.

silappathikaram:26:172-181.reading: When the envoys have gone, the ruler of the sea-girt earth, hailed by the lords of the land, leaves his camp, crosses to the northern bank of the Ganga on the Kannar's boats, is received by them, passes through their country and enters the northern land, making camp in enemy territory.
silappathikaram:26:172-181.unit_note: Start unchanged at line 172; end moved from line 184 to line 181: the crossing and the camp in enemy land close at line 181, and the list of enemy kings begins at line 182.
silappathikaram:26:172-181.event: The Chera crosses the Ganga on the Kannar's boats and camps in the enemy's northern country.

silappathikaram:26:182-199.reading: Before him Uttaran, Vichitran, Rudran, Bhairavan, Chitran, Singan, Dhanuttaran, Svetan and all the kings of the north, saying they will see the strength of southern Tamil, come on in league with Kanaka and Vijaya, and the king falls on them like a lion that, hunting, sees a herd of elephants, while drums, conches and horns shake every quarter and archers, spearmen, charioteers, elephant riders and horsemen close in.
silappathikaram:26:182-199.nuance: The northern kings take up the very phrase of the quarrel, தென்றமிழ் ஆற்றல் காண்குதும், so the battle is staged as a test of Tamil power. The drum that eats the offering of lives (உயிர்ப்பலி யுண்ணும்) makes the war itself a rite.
silappathikaram:26:182-199.unit_note: Start moved from line 185 to line 182 and end from line 201 to line 199: the list of enemy kings begins at line 182, and the lines 200-203 on the dust that silences bells and conches form one sentence with the next unit.
silappathikaram:26:182-199.event: The northern kings, allied with Kanaka and Vijaya, march to test Tamil strength and the Chera attacks.

silappathikaram:26:200-210.reading: The great dust of battle blinds the earth and stills the tongues of the elephants' bells and the conches, garlands tangle with garlands, archers' shoulders and heads lie severed in heaps, headless trunks stumble over corpses, and demon women dance to the drum and loosen their hair in the fat-laden blood that carries the bodies.
silappathikaram:26:200-210.unit_note: Start moved from line 202 to line 200 (see the previous unit) and end from line 213 to line 210: the description of the carnage closes at line 210, and line 211 begins the sentence on the Aryan kings' armies.

silappathikaram:26:211-224.reading: The king slays the fighting men of the Aryan kings and heaps them on the field, lays waste their chariots, elephants and horses so that the Aryan kings learn on the battlefield that the buffalo-rider eats a whole host of lives in a single day, wears the thumbai with the palmyra after the war dance, and Kanakan and Vijayan, who scorned rich Tamil trusting their swords, fall with fifty-two chariot warriors into Senguttuvan's net of anger.
silappathikaram:26:211-224.nuance: Death (the buffalo-rider) is made the Chera's teacher: the Aryan kings learn in one day what they did not know of Tamil strength. The capture, not the killing, of Kanakan and Vijayan keeps them for the humiliation that follows (they will carry the stone).
silappathikaram:26:211-224.unit_note: Start moved from line 214 to line 211 and end from line 228 to line 224: the sentence on the Aryan kings' armies begins at line 211, and the capture of Kanakan and Vijayan closes with படுதலும் on line 224.
silappathikaram:26:211-224.event: Senguttuvan destroys the Aryan kings' armies and captures Kanakan and Vijayan with fifty-two chariot warriors.

silappathikaram:26:225-246.reading: The other northern kings throw away their swords and slip off wherever they wish in disguise, as matted ascetics, robed monks, ash-smeared devotees, peacock-feather vow-keepers, singers, players and dancers, while the elephant-riding guardians tremble; and the demons praise the battlefield of the sword-ploughman who threshed it with tuskers yoked and the sword for goad, sing of the churning of the sea, the war in Lanka and the dark god's chariot war, dance the kuravai before and behind the chariot, and cook a meat-rice in pots on hearths of crowned heads stirred with bangled arms, which the demon cook serves, hailing the one who made a field of dharma by the victory of the just sceptre.
silappathikaram:26:225-246.nuance: The disguises cover the whole range of ascetics (matted hair, robes, ash, the peacock-feather fan of the great vow) and performers, so the defeated kings survive by wearing the marks of renunciation and art; the text says only that they went where they wished, not that the victor spared them knowingly. The demons' blessing calls the slaughter an அறக்களம் made by the செங்கோல்: the battle feast is given the name of dharma by those who eat it. விச்சைக் கோலத்து (the guise of the arts they had mastered) is not certain in sense.
silappathikaram:26:225-246.unit_note: Start unchanged at line 225; end moved from line 244 to line 246: the demons' feast and blessing, begun at line 240, close with ஊழி வாழ்கென on line 246.
silappathikaram:26:225-246.event: The surviving northern kings flee in the guise of ascetics and performers, and the demons sing and cook their battle feast for the victor.

claims.claim: a war won under a just sceptre makes the battlefield a field of dharma

silappathikaram:26:247-254.reading: Kuttuvan, having finished the battle, orders that the northern guardians of the Vedas, whose cool life keeps the great fire unquenched, be protected, sends out his many armies under Villavan Kothai to complete the conquest, and takes from the golden-peaked Himalaya the stone for the peerless pathini.
silappathikaram:26:247-254.nuance: Only now is the god of the vow (line 14) named: the stone is for the பத்தினி, Kannaki. The order to protect the Veda-keepers keeps the charge of the sky-faring sages (lines 102-103). காற்றூதாளர், those who blow the fire, is a rare word for the fire-tending Brahmins.
silappathikaram:26:247-254.unit_note: Start moved from line 245 to line 247 (see the previous unit); end unchanged at line 254.
silappathikaram:26:247-254.event: Senguttuvan orders the northern Brahmins protected, sends his armies on with Villavan Kothai, and takes the stone for the pathini from the Himalaya.

claims.claim: a conquering king must protect the Veda-keeping Brahmins of the conquered land

links.note: The vow to bring a stone for a god on the northern kings' heads is kept when the king takes the Himalayan stone after capturing Kanakan and Vijayan.
links.teaches: The vow names only a god to be carved and a royal insult to be avenged, and the close names the stone as the pathini's, so the epic joins a war of royal honour to the worship of Kannaki only once the vow is kept.

links.note: Both are royal vows in the conditional form whose penalty is the king's own sceptre turning cruel to his people; the Chera's line almost repeats the Pandya's.
links.teaches: The Pandya's vow names only his own subjects as the sufferers of a failed king, while the Chera's sets the choice out plainly, a sceptre that makes either foreign kings or his own people tremble, showing that the vow form took the king's power to terrify as fixed and staked the people's peace on a war abroad.

gains.a: the Chera's penalty clause is shown to be the old vanjinam formula, குடிபழி தூற்றும் கோலேன் ஆகுக, carried almost word for word into குடிநடுக் குறூஉங் கோலேன் ஆகென
gains.b: the formula gains a use against an insult reported from far away by ascetics rather than spoken to the king's face, so the vow answers a rumour of scorn

links.note: Both kings open a northern march by moving sword and umbrella at a chosen hour: the Chola with his drum to find foes for his arms, the Chera toward the Himalaya for a stone.
links.teaches: The Chola went north wanting only enemies for his shoulders, was stopped by the mountain and left his tiger carved on it, while the Chera goes with a cause, a pathini and an insult to Tamil, and carries a stone away from the mountain, so the epic's second northern march gives a moral reason to the rite the first performed for glory alone.

links.note: The couplet says the six-duty men forget their books if the guardian does not guard; the sages charge the Chera to guard the Veda-keepers of the Himalaya, which lies outside his kingdom.
links.teaches: The couplet ties the Brahmins' learning to their own king's protection, and the epic stretches that duty across the border, so that a king marching to punish northern kings is made guardian of the northern Brahmins, and he keeps the charge in victory (lines 248-250).

gains.a: the sages' charge gains a reason: without a guardian the Veda-keepers' learning fails, so the Chera's protection keeps the northern Vedas alive
gains.b: the couplet gains a case beyond the king's own realm, where the guardian of learning is an invader and the protection is owed to the enemy's Brahmins

links.note: Both cook a battlefield meal on hearths of crowned heads stirred with bangled arms (முடித்தலை அடுப்பு, தொடித்தோள் துடுப்பு), and both set it beside the king's care for Vedic Brahmins.
links.teaches: The puram poem makes the battlefield cooking the Pandya's own rite beside his completed Vedic sacrifices, and the epic gives the cooking to demons who call the field an அறக்களம் and then has the king order the fire-keeping Brahmins protected, so the epic keeps the old pairing of war-rite and Vedic rite and adds the name of dharma to the slaughter.

gains.a: the demons' feast is recognised as the formal battlefield sacrifice of the Pandya praise poem, not loose description of gore
gains.b: the puram image gains a later life in which the cooks are demons and the field is named a field of dharma, showing the formula become a convention that could be given to any Tamil conqueror

links.note: The couplet's spy goes in the guise of renouncers to get in and see; the defeated northern kings put on the guise of ascetics and performers to get away.
links.teaches: The couplet treats the renouncer's dress as a tool of the king's intelligence, and the epic shows the same dress used by kings themselves to escape a lost battle, so the guise that hides a spy's purpose also hides a king's shame, and it works because no one strikes a man who looks like a renouncer.

gains.a: the kings' flight gains a known device, the renouncer's dress as cover for passing through hostile ground, rather than a chance escape
gains.b: the couplet's technique gains a case where it is used not by a servant to enter but by the defeated to leave, turning a spy's skill into a mark of a king's disgrace

links.note: The patikam's second moral, that the great praise a renowned pathini, begins to be acted out when the Chera takes the stone for the pathini from the Himalaya.
links.teaches: The patikam promises only that the high will praise the pathini, and this kaathai shows the praise has to be won by humbling northern kings, so the honour paid to Kannaki and the Chera's conquest are made one act.

links.note: The decade's preface says Senguttuvan went for the stone of the goddess pathini, defeated the Aryan lord and bathed the stone in the Ganga; the kaathai tells the expedition at length. The epic here does not name the king's parents, so the identity rests on name and deed.
links.teaches: The preface compresses the campaign to a stone sought, one Aryan lord defeated and a bathing in the Ganga, while the epic gives the war a cause in an insult to Tamil, names two kings Kanakan and Vijayan, and brings the army over the Ganga on allies' boats, so the two show a shared tradition of the pathini's stone told with different enemies and routes.

gains.a: the epic's campaign gains an independent notice in the Chera decade's preface, showing the stone for the pathini was part of the Chera king's remembered deeds
gains.b: the preface's bare clause கடவுட் பத்தினிக் கற்கோள் gains its story: why the stone was sought, from whom it was taken, and that the god was Kannaki

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 253, பத்தினிக் கற்கால்)

new_concepts.gloss: the great rice offered and shared before battle, binding warriors to the king
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 49, பெருஞ்சோறு வகுத்து)

source_issues: The kaathai header gives a printed last line of 250 against 254 lines held.
Line 8 உயந்த்தோங்கு is probably a misprint for உயர்ந்தோங்கு.
Line 57 இறைஞ்சாக் சென்னி has a wrong sandhi consonant; the sense requires இறைஞ்சாச் சென்னி.
Line 179 ஒங்குநீர் has a short ஒ where ஓங்குநீர் is expected.
Every unit boundary was moved to a sense break; the cut units split speeches and lists at lines 22, 69, 94, 106, 128, 139, 149, 168, 184, 201, 213 and 244.
